claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy initially has a homogeneous FCC matrix.
The as-fabricated alloy contains inherent residual stresses.
The as-fabricated alloy contains fine microstructural features.
The as-fabricated alloy contains minor inclusions originating from additive manufacturing.
Degradation is governed by two competing, ambient-gas-dependent microstructural pathways.
In an O2-rich atmosphere, Cr and Ti oxidize selectively and preferentially at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary oxidation produces brittle oxide precipitates.
The grain-boundary oxides weaken intergranular cohesion and cause intergranular embrittlement and cracking.
Oxidation-induced intergranular embrittlement can culminate in catastrophic failure.
A reducing H2- or CO-rich atmosphere leaves the alloy without a substantial protective oxide layer.
The absence of a protective oxide layer in reducing gas promotes abnormal internal elemental redistribution.
Reducing exposure triggers phase segregation within the FCC matrix.
Reducing exposure may cause dealloying within the FCC matrix.
Internal segregation or dealloying destabilizes the matrix and reduces the cohesion needed to resist catastrophic failure.
At approximately 900 °C, continuous oxidizing exposure will produce oxide phases detectable by diffraction and microscopy.
At approximately 900 °C, continuous oxidizing exposure will produce intergranular cracks.
After switching from oxidizing to reducing gas at approximately 900 °C, the alloy will show pronounced internal phase segregation relative to the as-fabricated baseline.
After switching from oxidizing to reducing gas, the sample will exhibit minimal grain-boundary oxidation.
The proposed gas-dependent degradation mechanisms apply over 700–1100 °C.
Failure to observe distinct oxidation-dominated and segregation-dominated microstructures under the two gas histories would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The switched sample is first oxidized specifically to promote grain-boundary oxidation, but the reducing-state mechanism assumes absence of a substantial oxide layer and the prediction expects minimal grain-boundary oxidation. No oxide-removal or reduction step is specified to reconcile these statements.
